ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (epilepsy) Consultation — Fyodor Dostoevsky — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four-week follow-up with neurology consultation; EEG and MRI reviewed and lamotrigine started

text.paragraph: Recurrent generalized convulsive seizures for many years, never treated, in a 43-year-old man new to the practice. Please confirm the diagnosis, classify the seizures and the epilepsy, review the EEG and MRI, and advise on antiseizure medicine, monitoring, and safety counseling. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within four weeks, on the same day as his four-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Do the history and tests confirm epilepsy, and how should the seizures and the epilepsy be classified?
What further tests are needed, such as a sleep-deprived or prolonged EEG?
Which antiseizure medicine do you recommend, with what titration and what monitoring?
What safety, driving, and SUDEP counseling should he have?
How should his sleep loss, gambling, and mood be taken into account in his epilepsy care?
What follow-up do you advise, and when should he be seen sooner?

text.paragraph: Mr. Dostoevsky, a 43-year-old writer, is seen at the request of Dr. Lindahl. He has had generalized convulsive seizures since early adulthood, never treated, now every four to six weeks. Most are unwitnessed; those described to him by bystanders are generalized tonic-clonic, lasting one to two minutes, with tongue biting and hours of confusion afterwards. He recalls no aura and no focal features, and he has had no myoclonic jerks, absences, or seizures in clusters. The most recent, three weeks ago, followed a night without sleep. Sleep loss is the clearest trigger. He has gambling disorder in early treatment and mild depressive and anxiety symptoms. He lives alone and does not drive. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November 1821 and died in St. Petersburg on 9 February 1881. [D]
Dostoevsky had epilepsy throughout his literary career; in 1863 he went abroad to seek expert advice from the neurologists Romberg and Trousseau. [D]

Accounts of when his epilepsy began and was diagnosed differ. One account places seizures in his student years (1838 to 1843), a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in 1844, and a diagnosis of epilepsy in 1849, shortly before he was taken to the prison at Omsk; another says the first symptoms appeared in early adulthood and the diagnosis came about a decade later; a third calls the onset controversial. [R]
He was sentenced to four years of forced labor at the Siberian prison in Omsk; his seizures worsened during his imprisonment, and by 1853 he was quite debilitated by epilepsy. [D]
He described lack of sleep, alcohol, and overwork as triggers of his seizures, and he felt that the illness had damaged his memory. [D]

The type of his epilepsy is disputed: it has been interpreted as temporolimbic epilepsy, as an idiopathic generalized epilepsy with minor temporal involvement, as a cryptogenic focal epilepsy of frontomedial or temporal origin, and, for the ecstatic onset he described, as insular in origin. [R]
Whether the ecstatic experience he described before some seizures, and gave to characters in his fiction, was an epileptic aura is disputed. [R]
He portrayed up to six characters with epilepsy in his fiction, from Murin in The Landlady (1847) to Smerdyakov in The Brothers Karamazov (1880). [D]

His passion for roulette began on a tour of Europe in 1863. He fell into a pattern of chasing his losses and often pawned belongings so that he could gamble further. He gambled at Wiesbaden, Baden-Baden, and Bad Homburg, and the compulsion caused repeated financial trouble for about ten years. [D]
After returning to Russia he wrote the novella The Gambler, set in a fictional spa town called Roulettenburg, in 26 days. [D]
One retrospective review links his gambling to his epilepsy: the stress of gambling, together with sleep deprivation, is described as aggravating his seizures. [R]

list.item: Epilepsy of unknown type (G40.909). Epilepsy is confirmed by many unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart; a normal EEG and MRI do not exclude it. Under the ILAE classification the seizures are generalized tonic-clonic seizures of unknown onset and the epilepsy is of unknown type, with unknown cause, because neither the history nor the tests show whether the seizures begin focally or in both hemispheres. A sleep-deprived EEG may still clarify this. Treatment is clearly indicated, because the recurrence risk is high and every generalized tonic-clonic seizure carries a risk of injury and of SUDEP. [S]

Choice of antiseizure medicine. For an epilepsy of unknown type the medicine should work for both focal and generalized seizures. Valproate is the most effective for generalized and unclassified epilepsy, but it causes weight gain, tremor, and liver and metabolic effects. Levetiracetam starts quickly but can cause irritability and low mood, a concern with his depressive symptoms and gambling. Lamotrigine is effective and well tolerated, has mood-stabilizing effects, and is not an enzyme inducer, but it must be increased slowly to lower the risk of a serious rash. After discussion he chose lamotrigine. [S]

Safety and SUDEP. Living alone, sleeping irregularly, and having uncontrolled generalized tonic-clonic seizures, some at night, are the main SUDEP risk factors. Good seizure control lowers the risk most. [S]

Gambling disorder and mood in relation to his epilepsy (F63.0). Nights at the tables mean lost sleep and missed doses, so his gambling and his seizures share triggers. Depression and anxiety are common in epilepsy, and all antiseizure medicines carry a warning about suicidal thoughts, which matters more because gambling disorder raises suicide risk. Lamotrigine has no interaction with the treatments planned for his gambling. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Lindahl's first-visit note and laboratory results; the routine EEG with photic stimulation and hyperventilation, which is normal with no epileptiform discharges; and the epilepsy-protocol MRI, which is normal with no hippocampal sclerosis, cortical malformation, or other lesion. [S]

list.item: Start lamotrigine today: 25 mg daily for two weeks, 50 mg daily for two weeks, 50 mg twice daily for one week, 75 mg twice daily for one week, then 100 mg twice daily; primary care to check for rash at each dose step. [S]
Stop lamotrigine and seek care the same day for any rash, mouth sores, fever, or swollen glands. [S]
Sleep-deprived EEG in about three weeks. [S]

A lamotrigine trough level once at steady state as his reference, and again only after a breakthrough seizure, if nonadherence is suspected, or when an interacting medicine is started; no routine blood count or liver tests on lamotrigine. [S]
No rescue medicine now, because his seizures are single and brief; review if they become prolonged or come in clusters. [S]
Bone health: vitamin D is adequate and lamotrigine is not an enzyme inducer, so no DXA scan. [S]
A seizure diary, regular sleep with no writing through the night, little alcohol, and pill organizer and phone alarms for adherence. [S]
No driving until he has been seizure-free for a sustained period and I have reviewed him; showers rather than baths, no swimming or climbing alone, and care with stoves and sharp tools. [S]
SUDEP discussed today; a written seizure action plan for friends, who should call 911 for a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures, injury, or seizures in water. [S]
PHQ-9 and a suicide-risk review in primary care at each visit; continue gambling-disorder treatment. [S]
Neurology review in about ten months, in January, or sooner after any breakthrough seizure; primary care manages the titration and monitoring in between. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Lindahl, who sees him the same day and will start the titration. The diagnosis, the choice of medicine, the rash warning, and SUDEP were explained to Mr. Dostoevsky, who agreed with the plan and received the titration schedule and seizure action plan in writing. [S]
Follow-up: Neurology review in January, or sooner after any breakthrough seizure; results of the sleep-deprived EEG to be sent to Dr. Lindahl. [S]
